01.note: A teaching of the Sages says that written blessings and amulets, even though they contain God's name and passages of Torah, are left to burn in a fire on Shabbat; so, the Sages said, those who write blessings are like those who burn the Torah. A man in Sidon was writing such blessings. Rabbi Yishmael was told and went to check. As Rabbi Yishmael climbed the ladder, the man sensed him coming and plunged his bundle of blessings into a basin of water. Rabbi Yishmael told him that the punishment for this second act was greater than for the first.
01.why: The Gemara is working out which sacred writings may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat, including scrolls in other languages; this teaching adds blessings and amulets to the texts that are not rescued.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who goes to check on the man writing blessings and rebukes him.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of their rulings.
Written charms worn for protection, which could contain names of God and verses from the Torah.
Here, written-out texts of prayers and blessings; the Sages of that time opposed writing them down.

02.note: Imma Shalom, wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel, lived near a Christian philosopher reputed not to take bribes. To mock and expose him, she secretly gave him a golden lamp, then came before him with her brother asking for a share of her father's estate. He ruled they should divide it. Rabban Gamliel said their Torah gives a daughter nothing where there is a son; the philosopher said the Torah of Moses had been replaced by a book where son and daughter inherit alike. Next day Rabban Gamliel gave him a Libyan donkey, and he ruled that the book had not come to change the Torah, so the daughter does not inherit. She said, 'May your light shine like a lamp'; Rabban Gamliel said, 'The donkey came and kicked the lamp.'
02.why: The Gemara has been discussing the books of heretics and whether they are saved from fire, and has just given Rabbi Yohanan's mocking name for the Christian Gospel, 'avon gilyon'; this story shows that name in use.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel; she gives the philosopher a golden lamp.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Imma Shalom's brother, who argues the case with her and gives the philosopher a donkey.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Imma Shalom's husband; named only to identify her.

terms.meaning: A wordplay on the Greek 'Evangelion' (the Gospel), meaning roughly 'the sinful page'.
Here a Christian judge or scholar living in their neighborhood, known for claiming he took no bribes.

03.note: Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef, son of Rabba, what his father had been most careful about. He answered: the ritual fringes. One day, while Rabba was climbing the stairs, a string of his fringes snapped, and he would not go on until it was replaced. Then Abaye begins his own boast about Torah scholars who finish a tractate; his statement continues past this story.
03.why: The Gemara is listing Sages who each named the commandment they kept most carefully, such as Rav Sheshet with phylacteries and Rav Nahman with fringes; Rabba's son adds his father's devotion to fringes.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who asks Rabba's son about his father.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rabba
people.about: Rabba's son, who tells what his father was careful about.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The father, who would not move on until his torn fringe string was replaced.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage whose own boast begins at the end of the passage.

terms.meaning: Knotted strings the Torah commands Jews to tie to the corners of a four-cornered garment.

03.flag: The story ends mid-sentence: Abaye's statement ('when I see a young Torah scholar who has completed a tractate...') is cut off and finishes in the next segment.

04.note: A rich gentile lived near a man called Yosef who cherishes Shabbat. Astrologers told the gentile that Yosef would end up consuming all his property, so he sold everything, bought a pearl and put it in his hat. Crossing a river, the wind blew the hat into the water and a fish swallowed it. The fish was caught late on Friday afternoon, and the townspeople sent the fishermen to Yosef, who always bought fine food for Shabbat. He bought it, cut it open, found the pearl and sold it for thirteen vessels of gold coins. An old man who met him said: one who lends to Shabbat, Shabbat repays him.
04.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how Sages honored Shabbat by preparing for it themselves; this story shows the reward for spending on Shabbat, and leads into the question of what merit makes people wealthy.

people.name: Yosef who cherishes Shabbat
people.about: A Jew known for buying fine food in honor of Shabbat.

people.name: the gentile
people.about: Yosef's rich neighbor, who tries to escape the astrologers' prediction.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday night.
Here called Chaldeans: people who foretold the future from the stars.

05.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, how the wealthy in lands without Sages earn their wealth. He answered: because they honor Shabbat, and cited Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba. Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba told of staying with a householder in Laodicea who was served at a gold table so heavy it took sixteen men to carry, hung with silver chains and set with dishes and every kind of food. When it was set down they recited 'The earth and all that fills it is God's,' and when it was taken away, 'The heavens are God's heavens, but the earth He gave to mankind.' Asked how he had earned this, the host said he had been a butcher who set aside the finest animal each time for Shabbat. Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba told him he was fortunate and blessed God for this merit.
05.why: This is the last of three answers: the wealthy of the Land of Israel earn it by tithing, those of Babylonia by honoring the Torah, and those elsewhere by honoring Shabbat, which this account is brought to prove.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who asks how the wealthy of different lands earn their wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who answers that they honor Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who stayed with the rich householder in Laodicea and tells the story.

terms.meaning: A city where Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba was a guest, outside the lands where the Sages lived.

06.note: A fire broke out on Shabbat in the courtyard of Yosef ben Simai in Shihin. Soldiers came from the fortress of Tzippori to put it out, because he was a steward of the king, but he would not let them, out of respect for Shabbat. A miracle happened: rain fell and put out the fire. That evening he sent two sela coins to each soldier and fifty to their commander. When the Sages heard, they said he need not have stopped them, citing the rule that one tells a gentile neither 'put it out' nor 'don't put it out.'
06.why: The mishna says a Jew need not tell a gentile to put out or leave a fire on Shabbat, and the Gemara has just argued over whether one may hint 'whoever puts it out will not lose'; this incident shows the Sages applying the mishna to a real fire.

people.name: Yosef ben Simai
people.about: A steward of the king whose courtyard caught fire on Shabbat and who refused the soldiers' help.

terms.meaning: A manager of the king's property or affairs.
A silver coin.
The core collection of the early Sages' rulings, which the Gemara discusses.

07.note: Rav Yehuda, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Hanan bar Rava came to stay at the house of Avin of Nashikiya. Beds were brought for the first two but not for Rav Hanan bar Rava. He then found Avin teaching his son the mishna that allows covering a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat. Rav Hanan said, 'Avin the fool is teaching his son folly,' arguing that the feces are food for dogs and may simply be moved. Avin asked how he should teach it instead, and Rav Hanan told him to say 'chicken feces.'
07.why: The mishna permits covering a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat; Rav Hanan's challenge to that very line opens the Gemara's discussion, which goes on to ask why such feces could not just be removed.

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Rava
people.about: A guest who is not given a bed and then mocks his host's teaching.

people.name: Avin
people.about: The host, from Nashikiya, who is teaching his son the mishna.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: One of the guests, who is given a bed.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: One of the guests, who is given a bed.

terms.meaning: The core collection of the early Sages' rulings; here, the ruling that one may cover a child's feces with a bowl on Shabbat.
Limits on how far people and things may be moved on Shabbat; Rav Hanan cites flowing water, which has none, to argue the feces count as ready for use.

08.note: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana reported that once a snake fell into the study hall on Shabbat, and a Nabatean stood up and killed it. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: 'One of its type killed it.'
08.why: The Gemara is debating whether snakes and scorpions may be killed on Shabbat; right after, it asks whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's remark meant the man had acted properly or not.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage, who remarks on the killing of the snake.

people.name: the Nabatean
people.about: A man of the Nabatean people who killed the snake.

terms.meaning: A member of a non-Jewish people of the region.

09.note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Manyomi, owed money to the household of the Exilarch, and they brought him there on Shabbat and tormented him to make him pay. Some spittle was on the floor, and the Exilarch told his household to bring a vessel and put it over the spittle. Abba bar Manyomi told them there was no need, since Rav Yehuda ruled that one may step on spittle in passing. The Exilarch said: he is a Torah scholar, leave him alone.
09.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Yehuda's ruling that one may tread on spittle on Shabbat without intending to smooth the ground; this story shows the ruling being quoted in practice.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Manyomi; a scholar who owed money to the Exilarch's household.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: Head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, whose household held Abba's debt.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

10.note: Shmuel came to the house of Avin Toran. A gentile came in and lit a lamp, and Shmuel turned his face away so as not to benefit from its light. When he saw the gentile bring a document and read it, Shmuel said the man had lit it for his own use, and turned his face back toward the lamp.
10.why: The Gemara is asking when a Jew may use a lamp a gentile lit on Shabbat, concluding that it depends on whom the gentile lit it for; Shmuel's behavior shows that test applied.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage visiting Avin Toran's house on Shabbat.

people.name: Avin Toran
people.about: The host whose house Shmuel visited.

11.note: Rava was walking along a street in Mehoza when his shoes got dirty with clay. His servant picked up a piece of broken pottery from the street and wiped them. The Sages there shouted at him. Rava said: is it not enough that they have not learned, they also teach others? If the shard were in a courtyard it could be used to cover a vessel; here too it is useful to me.
11.why: Rava has just ruled, against Shmuel and Rav Nahman, that a small pottery shard may be moved on Shabbat even in the public domain; this story shows him acting on that view.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose servant wipes his shoes with a shard on Shabbat.

people.name: Rava's servant
people.about: Wipes the clay off Rava's shoes with a shard from the street.

terms.meaning: A broken piece of an earthenware pot.
In Shabbat law, a street or open area used by the public, as opposed to a private courtyard.

12.note: Rav Dimi reported in Rabbi Hanina's name that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once came to a place and found a row of building stones. He told his students to go and have in mind to sit on them the next day, Shabbat, without doing anything to the stones. Rabbi Yohanan disagreed: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did require an action. Rabbi Ami said he told them to arrange the stones; Rabbi Asi said he told them to rub off the mortar.
12.why: Rabba and Rav Yosef disagree whether an object set aside from use on Shabbat needs an action, or only a thought, to make it usable; the Gemara shows Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi holding the same split views in their versions of this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage, who tells his students to prepare the stones for sitting on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required an action, not just a thought.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Says the instruction was to arrange the stones.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Says the instruction was to rub the mortar off them.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brought the report from the Land of Israel to Babylonia.

terms.meaning: Things not meant for use on Shabbat, which therefore may not be moved then unless prepared beforehand.

13.note: Rabba reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once came to a place too crowded for his students, went out to a field full of sheaves of grain and cleared the whole field. Rav Yosef reported the same incident about Rabbi Hiyya: he too found the place too crowded, went out to a field of sheaves and cleared all of it.
13.why: The mishna lets one move four or five baskets of produce on Shabbat to make room for guests, and the Gemara asks whether more is allowed for more guests; these reports prove it depends on the number of guests.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage who, in one version, clears a field to make room for students.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who, in the other version, clears the field.

terms.meaning: Bundles of cut grain stalks.

14.note: A man from the Upper Galilee worked three years for a householder in the south. On the eve of Yom Kippur he asked for his wages to feed his family. To every request, for money, produce, land, animals or bedding, the householder said 'I have none,' and the worker went home in anguish. After Sukkot the householder brought the wages and three donkeys loaded with food, drink and sweets. After they ate, he asked what the worker had suspected; for each refusal the worker had imagined an innocent reason, ending with 'perhaps he consecrated all his property to Heaven.' The householder swore it was so: he had vowed away his property because his son Hyrcanus would not study Torah, and the Sages had released his vows. He said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
14.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just listed judging others favorably among the deeds whose reward is enjoyed in this world as well as the next; this teaching, that one who judges others favorably is judged favorably, is illustrated by the worker.

people.name: the worker
people.about: A man from the Upper Galilee who worked three years without pay and judged his employer favorably.

people.name: the householder
people.about: The employer who said he had nothing, then came to pay with gifts.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: The householder's son, who did not study Torah.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
Given to the Temple; property dedicated this way could not be used or paid out to anyone.
The Sages had the power to annul a vow that a person regretted.
Produce from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor had been taken; untithed produce may not be eaten or given.

15.note: A pious man redeemed a young Jewish woman from captivity. At the inn he had her sleep at his feet. The next morning he went down, immersed in a ritual bath, and taught his students. He asked what they had suspected when she lay at his feet; they said perhaps one of the students was not trusted and he wanted to protect her. He asked what they had suspected when he immersed; they said perhaps the strain of the journey had caused him a seminal emission. He swore by the Temple service that this was so, and said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
15.why: This is the second in a run of teachings about judging others favorably, following the worker who imagined innocent reasons for his employer's refusals; here students do the same for their teacher.

people.name: the pious man
people.about: A man who redeemed a captive woman and later asked his students what they had suspected of him.

terms.meaning: A pool of water used for immersion to become ritually pure.
A discharge of semen, which made a man ritually impure until he immersed.
An oath formula, swearing by the worship once done in the Temple in Jerusalem.

16.note: The Torah scholars needed something from a Roman matron whom all the great men of Rome visited, and asked who would go. Rabbi Yehoshua said he would. With his students, he took off his phylacteries four cubits from her door, went in and locked the door behind him. When he came out he immersed in a ritual bath and taught his students. He asked what they had suspected at each step; they answered that holy objects may not enter an impure place, that perhaps there was a royal matter between them, and that perhaps some of her spittle had sprayed onto his clothes. He swore by the Temple service that this was so, and said: as you judged me favorably, so may God judge you favorably.
16.why: This is the third teaching in a row about students judging a teacher favorably when his conduct looked suspicious; the Gemara then returns to the mishna's list of what may be moved on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who goes to the matron and then asks his students what they suspected of him.

terms.meaning: A noble Roman woman, here one with influence among the great men of Rome.
Small leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; in Hebrew, tefillin.
About two meters; a cubit is a forearm's length.
The Sages ruled that a gentile's spittle is ritually impure, which is why he would immerse if it touched his clothes.

17.note: Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava's wife, immersed in a ritual bath within thirty days of giving birth, while her husband was not with her. She caught cold, and her funeral bier was brought after Rava to Pumbedita.
17.why: Shmuel said a woman after childbirth has a thirty-day rule, which the Sages of Neharde'a read as a ban on immersing in that time because of the cold; Rava limits it to when her husband is away, and cites this incident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage; his wife's death follows her immersion while he was away.

people.name: Rav Hisda's daughter
people.about: Rava's wife, who immersed within thirty days of childbirth and caught cold.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Her father.

terms.meaning: Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure, required of a woman after childbirth before marital relations resume.
The frame on which a body is carried to burial.

18.note: After Shmuel had blood let, a teak armchair was broken up for him to make a fire. For Rav Yehuda an ebony table was broken up, and for Rabba a bench.
18.why: Shmuel ruled that a fire may be made on Shabbat even in summer for someone who caught cold after bloodletting; these Sages had furniture burned for that purpose. Next Abaye asks Rabba whether breaking the bench was wasteful destruction.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage for whom a teak armchair was burned after bloodletting.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage for whom an ebony table was burned.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage for whom a bench was burned.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in that era; afterward a person was thought to be weak and prone to chills.

19.note: The gentile scholar Ablat found Shmuel lying in the sun. He asked: 'Wise man of the Jews, can something harmful be good?' Shmuel answered: it is a day of bloodletting.
19.why: The Gemara has just advised someone too poor to eat after bloodletting to lie in the sun; Shmuel is found doing so. Right after, the Gemara says his answer hid the truth: he did not want to reveal that the solstice sun is the beneficial one.

people.name: Ablat
people.about: A gentile scholar who questions Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage found lying in the sun after bloodletting.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in that era.

20.note: Shmuel used to have blood let in a house whose walls were seven and a half bricks thick. One day after bloodletting he felt weak. He checked and found that a half-brick was missing from the wall.
20.why: Rav and Shmuel have just warned that someone who has blood let should not sit in the wind, lest it draw out more blood; this story shows even a small gap in a wall affecting Shmuel himself.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who felt weak after bloodletting and found a gap in the wall.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in that era.
